finding.title: Task-level Python verification runs Host Python on device-started or device-approved work, bypassing the start gate and the Host-wide review gate
finding.scenario: Workstation plans a localOnly mission: step 0 is filesystem.write of hello.py with content print("BUNNY_A_OK"); step 1 is an Ollama model step with verification task_spec {kind:python,name:hello.py,expected:BUNNY_A_OK}. Workstation approves with start=false. A paired device calls mission.start (commands.server.ts:60 calls deviceStartRefusal). deviceStartRefusal builds operations only from capability executors and capability verifications (manager.server.ts:2199-2202) and never inspects task_spec, so it returns null and the start is accepted. The device-attributed hello.py write is recorded as an unreviewed paired-device change. When the Ollama Task completes, the Task carries verify (manager.server.ts:1356, attached for workstation envelopes; only remote envelopes strip it), and TaskManager runs verifySpec (host manager.server.ts:1460) which calls exec('python',[hello.py]) (verification.server.ts:59) with no pendingRemoteChanges check. Python therefore executes on the Host. Direct variant: a workstation-submitted direct local Task with verify python parks in waiting_for_approval; a device approve passes deviceMayLaunch (http.server.ts approve case, lines 556-570) and the Host runs the same python.
finding.evidence: Throwaway probe in an OS-temp mkdtemp folder (deleted): device mission.start returned state running; child verify={kind:python,name:hello.py,expected:BUNNY_A_OK}; pending device change hello.py present before and after the run; event verification.completed 'Bunny-A ran python ... hello.py: stdout="BUNNY_A_OK", exit_code=0'. Direct probe: submitted state waiting_for_approval, deviceMayLaunch true, after tasks.approve(device) state completed with the same python run. grep shows no python/task_spec device case in remote-authority.test.ts or missions.test.ts. Same root cause, not probed: agent.resume via deviceResumeRefusal -> deviceStartRefusal (agent-runtime.server.ts:211-214) and device provider.execute answers via deviceRequestRefusal (manager.server.ts:2051). Payload note: the .py content is the workstation-planned one-liner and a device cannot author .py (filesystem.write is inert-only), so the device triggers execution rather than choosing code; this still violates 'never authorize Python execution' and control (A) that no code run starts while a paired-device change is unacknowledged.
finding.recommendation: In deviceStartRefusal and deviceRequestRefusal, treat every verification that executes code (python task_spec, command, git_diff_nonempty) as code: refuse device start, resume and answers when any such check exists on a workstation envelope. In verifySpec's python branch, require pendingRemoteChanges() to be empty and refuse when the Task's Mission is device-driven or the approving actor is a device. Add device-authority tests for python task_spec under start, resume, provider.execute answer and direct approve.

Its only skill check is for a skill step under EXECUTE, and a model step with a task_spec python check passes. The gate returns null.

The Ollama route is tool-free, so manager.server.ts:1452 never consults pendingRemoteReview for it. Nothing checks pendingRemoteChanges before the Host python run.

The device does choose the start timing and triggers real Host Python execution, which matches the BLOCKER definition in the brief.

Mitigations I checked that do not refute it: the python source must be exactly print("<expected>") (verifySpec line ~62), and a device cannot write a .py file (authorization.server.ts:245 inertDataPath). That bounds the payload but does not satisfy control (A), which states that no non-direct Bunny code run starts while a paired-device change is unacknowledged, nor the start gate's own rule. It is therefore a policy violation on the authoritative control, and the rubric's BLOCKER wording (device causes code execution) literally matches. Severity could be argued as HIGH given the bounded payload; I kept BLOCKER per the rubric definition.

finding.title: Git reads and gh reads run on workstation-envelope work that a device starts or answers
finding.scenario: deviceStartRefusal evaluates only operations where runsCode is true (manager.server.ts:2208). runsCode (authorization.server.ts:250) excludes read-only Git (git.status/diff/log and the other git.* READ actions) and github.* READ actions. remoteExecutionRefusal (authorization.server.ts:229) refuses only GIT_MUTATIONS for Git. Git reads are unhardened for workstation envelopes: local.server.ts:206 applies core.fsmonitor=false, hooksPath, diff.external and --no-textconv only when context.remoteAuthority is set, which bus.server.ts sets only for remote envelopes. Probe: a repo whose owner config sets diff.drv.textconv to a node one-liner that writes a marker file, with .gitattributes data.x diff=drv; the workstation approves a plan with one git.diff step; the device's mission.start is accepted; the mission completes; the marker file is written, so the owner-configured textconv ran on the device's start. The same class applies to device answers of git.* asks (remoteExecutionRefusal does not cover read-only Git) and to github.* reads, which run gh with git children.
finding.evidence: Throwaway probe in an OS-temp folder (deleted): device mission.start accepted, mission state completed, steps [[Reviewer,completed]], owner-configured textconv executed (true). Payload is owner-configured repo config: a device cannot write .git (touchesGitMetadata) or .gitattributes (executionConfigPath denylist), so the device chooses timing, not content. When paired-device changes are pending, the bus.server.ts review gate (git./github. prefix) would hold the read, so the gap is the no-pending-change case.
finding.recommendation: Classify Git reads and github.* reads as code-running in runsCode (or add them to the device start and answer refusals) for workstation envelopes started or answered by a device, or run them hardened (the remoteAuthority flags) for any device-driven authority. Add a device-start test with a textconv driver.

votes.reasoning:
The gap is real but its impact is narrower than the claimed HIGH.

Verified in code (no repo files edited, no tests run, no probes run):
- manager.server.ts:2208 `if (!runsCode(action, params, risk)) continue;` skips every operation that is not terminal.exec, a GIT_MUTATIONS action, or a non-Calculator EXECUTE. git.status/diff/log/tracked_files/branch/commit_info and github.* READ actions therefore never reach the decision check, so deviceStartRefusal returns null for a workstation envelope whose only code-running path is Git reads.
- authorization.server.ts:250 runsCode confirms this classification. The deviceStartRefusal doc comment (manager.server.ts ~2170) says a workstation envelope carrying "hook-running Git" is started on the workstation, so the implementation misses the stated design for read-only Git.
- local.server.ts:206 applies core.fsmonitor=false, hooksPath, diff.external= and --no-textconv only when context.remoteAuthority is set. bus.server.ts:322 sets remoteAuthority only for remote envelopes, so workstation-envelope git.status and git.diff run owner-configured fsmonitor, textconv and external-diff programs unhardened. The git.diff path (local.server.ts ~236-241) runs `git diff --stat` and `git diff` with no textconv suppression.
- bus.server.ts:169 gates git./github. requests only when remoteReviewFor returns a pending paired-device review, so the no-pending-change case is ungated.

Why the severity is MEDIUM, not HIGH:
- The program run is owner-configured (.git/config and .gitattributes are denied to device writes via touchesGitMetadata and executionConfigPath). The device chooses timing, not content.
- Textconv only fires for tracked files that differ from the index. A clean tree runs nothing, and a file the device dirties itself triggers the review gate (git. prefix) before the run. The bare case needs owner-side dirty files that match a driver.
- The escalation to device-chosen code needs an interpreter-style textconv applied to a device-writable inert extension, which is an unusual owner setup. I did not verify that path.
- The claimant's probe is not reproduced here. The code-path reading above is independently confirmed.

It is not refuted: it contradicts the stated deviceStartRefusal design and the policy's "indirect capabilities" language, so it stays a real correctness and policy gap.

Not refuted: the precondition holds, but I rate it MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

The start path is commands.server.ts:60 (markDeviceDriven after the refusal check).

The plan containing git.diff was workstation-approved. The device controls only timing, plus the content of device-written inert files, and those writes are already gated by the pending-change review (bus.server.ts:169). It is still a real classifier gap against the stated policy (unknown or indirect execution through a READ-classified capability), and it is inconsistent with the remote path, which hardens textconv and fsmonitor. Note the accepted limitation "Git reads under remote authority run owner-configured filter drivers" covers only remote authority, not this workstation-envelope case, so it does not dispose of it.

finding.title: Review prompt escapes changed-file content but not changed-file paths
finding.scenario: NTFS names may contain U+202E (RLO) or U+2028/U+2029; Win32 forbids control characters 0-31, so newline injection into the listing is not possible. Line 2343 builds the review listing with JSON.stringify(path), which leaves U+202E raw, unlike describeRemoteChange which escapes bidi and line-separator characters for content. A device can therefore write an inert file whose name contains U+202E so the workstation prompt displays a reversed or misleading name. Line 3488 (the desktop ask reason) joins raw paths from remoteChanges with ', ' and does no encoding at all.
finding.evidence: Probe: JSON.stringify of a string with U+202E returns the character unescaped (code points 22 72 65 70 202e 6f 72 74 2e 74 78 74 22). Content and digest in the same listing remain correct. Display-only misdirection of the approval target name; not a code-execution path.
finding.recommendation: Apply the same U+2028/U+2029/U+202A-202E/U+2066-2069 escaping to paths in pendingRemoteReview (line 2343) and JSON-encode the paths joined at line 3488.

votes.reasoning: Not refuted. The core claim is accurate and reproduced. manager.server.ts:2343 builds the listing with JSON.stringify(path), and a probe (temp mkdtemp folder, deleted afterwards) showed U+202E (code point 202e) passes through raw. Content is protected: describeRemoteChange (manager.server.ts:74-82) escapes U+2022, U+2028/2029, U+202A-202E and U+2066-2069 in the file preview, so only the name is unescaped. The device-chosen name reaches the listing via recordRemoteChange (line 185) and pendingRemoteChanges, and filesystem.write (capabilities/local.server.ts:39) accepts any name that scopedPath allows. The desktop ask reason at manager.server.ts:3488 joins raw paths with ", " and has no encoding, so a crafted name can also imitate prompt prose there, including the "Review them before allowing" sentence. Limits on impact: the approval binds the pending change ids and the SHA-256 digest, not the display name; the file's real content and digest are shown beneath the name; a device still cannot cause code execution (writes are limited to data/document types and any run still needs a workstation grant). So the effect is approver-display misdirection (LOW), which is not an owner-policy disposition. I did not edit anything in the repo and did not run any test, so test-results/ is unchanged.

The defect is real, not refutable. Verified in code: manager.server.ts:2343 builds the review listing with JSON.stringify(path), and describeRemoteChange (line 81) applies the bidi/line-separator escape only to file content. Probe: JSON.stringify leaves U+202E (202e) and U+2028 (2028) raw in a path string. A device can name a file with those characters via filesystem.write (scopedPath accepts any name; NTFS allows them; Windows only forbids control characters 0-31 and <>:"|?*). recordRemoteChange stores the resolved absolute path (line 180-185), so the device-chosen name appears in the listing. The second part is also accurate: the desktop ask reason at lines 3486-3488 joins raw run.params.path strings from remoteChanges (lines 2306-2312) with no JSON or bidi encoding, and those raw params are not normalized to the resolved file path. Impact is display-only: an RLO in the name can visually reorder the rest of that prompt line, including the size, digest and content JSON, and a crafted name can imitate reason text. It does not cause code execution or action outside the envelope. Acknowledgement is by change id, not by name; content and SHA-256 are shown escaped for content; and the review gate requires every pending change to be acknowledged before code runs. It is inconsistent with the round-10 (H) intent that file text cannot imitate prompt structure, so LOW is the right severity. Not one of the listed dispositions. No test or repo files were modified; the probe ran in a deleted mkdtemp folder.

finding.title: Shell-session review prompt omits the paired-device change content; the workstation acknowledges unshown changes
finding.scenario: A device writes an inert data file (for example notes.md or notes2.md) under paired-device authority. The Host-wide review gate then holds any shell-capable provider session. For a remote envelope, taskViolation() already returns the DESKTOP_REQUIRED text for every shell child (authorization.server.ts:483 and 496-498, via providerScopeViolation -> remoteSessionViolation), so at dispatch the reason is `violation ?? agenticViolation ?? reviewViolation` (line 1469) and the review listing built at line 1453 (size, SHA-256, content) is discarded. The request still carries remoteReview = review.ids (line 1463-1472). The prompt text comes from askPermission's deviceChanges, which uses the mission-scoped remoteChanges(mission) (manager.server.ts:3486), so it names only this Mission's paths, and names none for a change made in another Mission. The workstation's allow_once then acknowledges the Host-wide review.ids (line 3709) and the shell session launches over the unshown file content. Result: code-capable agent or session authority runs over device-written content the workstation never saw, which defeats the authoritative control in policy item (A).
finding.evidence: Probe (node --experimental-strip-types, repo modules imported by file URL, fresh temp Host, claude adapter stub, phone actor device:r12-phone): (1) In-Mission case: device-driven mission with a filesystem.write notes.md step then a claude access:write model step. Ask: desktopRequired=true, remoteReview=[1 id], reason = "claude for Coder: Approval required on Windows Host: a paired device cannot authorize command or code execution. claude write sessions run with shell authority. Files changed in this Mission under paired-device authority: notes.md. Review them before allowing." Regex check for sha256/full content/body text in reason: false. After workstation respond allow_once: sessions launched = 1, pendingRemoteChanges = 0. (2) Cross-Mission case: device wrote notes2.md in mission A (completed). Mission B has only the claude write model step. Ask reason = "claude for Coder: Approval required on Windows Host: ... claude write sessions run with shell authority." with no file name; remoteReview=[1 id]; after allow_once: sessions launched = 1, pendingRemoteChanges = 0. The existing test file (72/72 passing) does not cover the dispatch-path reason for a remote shell child with a pending review. Workstation-envelope variant: the same dropped-listing path applies whenever taskViolation (for example provider-session budget exhausted) is non-null alongside a pending review (same line 1469; code-path inference, not probed).
finding.recommendation: Never let the violation text replace the review listing: when review is non-null, build the reason as the violation text plus reviewViolation (listing included), and attach remoteReview only for ids whose path and content are in that listing. In askPermission (line 3486) name the exact remoteReview paths instead of the mission-scoped remoteChanges. Add a regression test: a cross-Mission pending change and a remote shell child must produce a reason containing the sha256 and the JSON content of the file, and allow_once must acknowledge only those ids. Add the same assertion for the violation-plus-review combination on a workstation envelope.

votes.reasoning:
Not refuted. The code path matches the finding, verified by reading (no probe run; no repo files edited; no tests run).

1. manager.server.ts:1439-1447 and 1452-1453: for a remote envelope, taskViolation() returns a non-null violation for a write/shell session. providerScopeViolation (authorization.server.ts ~483) calls remoteSessionViolation (authorization.server.ts:217-222), which returns DESKTOP_REQUIRED text whenever the session authority is outside REMOTE_SESSION_CEILING. Claude/shell write sessions fall outside it.

2. manager.server.ts:1469 builds the ask reason as `violation ?? agenticViolation ?? reviewViolation`. When violation is non-null, reviewViolation (the only text carrying review.listing, i.e. size, sha256 and JSON content) is dropped. The same happens for a workstation envelope when the provider-session budget is exhausted (violation non-null, remoteSession = reviewViolation, reason still excludes the listing).

3. askPermission (manager.server.ts:3486-3488) appends only remoteChanges(mission), which is mission-scoped (manager.server.ts:2306-2313) and returns [] for non-remote envelopes. So the prompt names this Mission's paths at most, and names nothing for a change from another Mission or for a workstation-envelope Mission.

4. Line 1471 still attaches remoteReview: review.ids, which is Host-wide. On allow_once by a workstation actor, manager.server.ts:3708-3709 acknowledges all of those ids, although their content was never in the prompt.

Result: the authoritative control in policy item (A) (full content and sha256 shown for each changed file, acknowledge only shown files) is not met on this path. Code-running authority (a shell-capable session) is granted over device-written content the workstation did not see.

Severity: I do not think BLOCKER is justified. The device cannot start the session itself; the workstation must still click allow_once on a desktopRequired request, and the session's shell authority is what the workstation approves. The defect is that the informed-review precondition is defeated on this path, which is HIGH. I did not probe the cross-Mission case end to end; the conclusion rests on the code reading above, which is unambiguous.

The defect is real; I did not refute it. I only read code and ran no probes or repo tests, and I changed no files.

Verified path:
- manager.server.ts:1452-1453 builds reviewViolation with review.listing (size, SHA-256, JSON content). Line 1463 sets remoteSession = remoteSessionViolation(task, envelope) ?? reviewViolation.
- Line 1469 builds the reason as `violation ?? agenticViolation ?? reviewViolation`, so the listing is dropped whenever an earlier violation is non-null.
- For a remote envelope, taskViolation (authorization.server.ts:483, 496-498) calls providerScopeViolation, which calls remoteSessionViolation (authorization.server.ts:217-223). That returns the DESKTOP_REQUIRED text for any shell-capable session. So for remote shell children the listing is discarded on every dispatch, not only in the cross-Mission case.
- askPermission (manager.server.ts:3486-3488) appends only names from remoteChanges(mission), which is mission-scoped (manager.server.ts:2306-2313). A change made in another Mission gets no file name in the prompt at all.
- Line 1463 still attaches remoteReview = review.ids, which is Host-wide. Respond (manager.server.ts:3709-3710) then acknowledges every id in that list when allow_once is given.

Net effect: the workstation can acknowledge and launch a shell session over paired-device content it was never shown. That defeats the policy's authoritative Host-wide review gate (item A). I would not rate it BLOCKER: the device cannot start execution by itself, because a workstation allow_once click is still required. The defect is an uninformed approval that fails open on every remote shell session. The reviewer's BLOCKER rating is arguable, so I rate it HIGH.

Suggested fix, as the finding states: build the reason from the listing when review is non-null, and attach remoteReview only for ids whose content was shown.

finding.title: Path-segment classifier refuses ordinary device data writes under dot-directories and node_modules
finding.scenario: executionConfigPath() tests every segment of the full absolute path (resolvedNames segments include the project root and its ancestors), not only the part below the project root. A project under C:/Users/allam/.codex/worktrees/abc/proj, .claude/, .config/, .cursor/, .vscode/, .github/ or node_modules/ therefore refuses every paired-device filesystem.write/delete of an inert file such as notes.txt with 'notes.txt configures Git, package scripts, hooks or tasks that run commands.' Probed: a plain notes.txt is allowed in C:/Users/allam/Documents/new/bun-router but refused under the ~/.codex, ~/.claude and node_modules paths. Fail-closed, so availability only; no authority is widened.
finding.evidence: Probe (node --experimental-strip-types, remoteExecutionRefusal, cwd variants): cwd=C:/Users/allam/Documents/new/bun-router -> null; cwd=C:/Users/allam/.codex/worktrees/abc/proj -> 'notes.txt configures Git, package scripts, hooks or tasks...'; same for .claude/projects and node_modules/somepkg/data. Call site: authorization.server.ts:241 (executionConfigPath(path) in remoteExecutionRefusal).
finding.recommendation: Evaluate the directory-segment and GIT_SEGMENT tests only on the path below the project/envelope root (the Mission root or envelope projectRoots entry that contains the path), so ancestors outside the project cannot trigger the refusal. Keep the full-path check only for leaf-file names and for Git metadata inside the project.

finding.title: Verification python runs are not covered by the Host-wide review gate

The Host then runs that script while the change is still pending. The executed source must equal the planned one-line print('<expected>') exactly (verification.server.ts source check), so no device-chosen code runs and I found no escalation. finding.title: Survivor lineage misses orphans whose intermediate parent exited between tree samples
finding.scenario: A workstation-approved provider session (write/shell) runs a short-lived intermediate (for example cmd /c start node server.js, or a shell wrapper with a trailing &). The intermediate exits within the 15 s tree-sampling window, so it never appears in task.processTree. The session root then exits. watchSurvivors builds its lineage only from {root} plus the stored snapshot, so the surviving grandchild (ppid = dead intermediate, which Windows keeps as the parent id) is never added. lingering stays empty, liveCodeExecutions() returns no live code, and remoteMutationHeld() returns null, so a paired-device filesystem.write of an inert file (.txt/.json/.md) lands while the workstation-approved process is still running and may load it. The review gate only covers code runs Bunny starts later, so it does not cover this window. Probe (read-only harness, synthetic process rows, TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors called on a fake this): (A) root exited, sampled child and grandchild alive -> survivors [200,300]; (B) intermediate never sampled, its child alive -> survivors []; (C) same as B with the intermediate sampled once -> survivors [500]; (D) root pid reused -> []. Scope note: this is close to the accepted limitation 'a process whose whole ancestor chain lived between two 15 s snapshots', but here the root was sampled and only the intermediate was missed, so the owner should decide whether it is covered. Impact depends on what the survivor loads; no code execution by the device was demonstrated.
finding.evidence: watchSurvivors lineage at manager.server.ts:1716-1718 (lineage = root + snapshot only); alive/grow loops 1719-1737 only admit rows whose ppid is already in lineage; tree sampling every 15000 ms in watchTree (1657-1690) with processTree updated only on change; hold uses liveCodeExecutions() at manager.server.ts:2404 (lingering entries from tasks.lingering). Probe run: node --experimental-strip-types harness against src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts, scenarios A-D as above; probe files deleted afterwards.
finding.recommendation: Close the window fail-closed: while a session runs, sample at a much shorter interval (about 1 s) or record every observed parent/child link so intermediates that die between samples are still in lineage; alternatively, when an attempt ends, treat any process created at or after the attempt's start time whose parent is unknown or dead as a live survivor until it exits. finding.title: Workstation one-time allow of a held device write lifts the hold for live code with no content review

The hold text promises that the change 'is then listed for review before code runs over it', but the review gate only applies to code runs that start later, and the write is not acknowledged. Live code that reads the new file therefore runs over content the workstation never saw. This is a deliberate workstation decision, so severity is LOW; it is reported because the prompt asks the workstation to review files it cannot read.

finding.evidence: Probe 1 (decide, pure): workstation envelope expired + oneTime -> allow; device-granted envelope expired + oneTime -> ask 'The remote mission authorization expired.'. Control without the device answer -> waiting_for_user, no write. Practical trigger needs a queued step at the expiry instant, so availability-timing dependent; no new action or scope is reached.
finding.recommendation: For one-time allowances from a paired device, re-check envelope.expiresAt (and revocation) before honoring oneTime, as the remote branch already does; alternatively clear approvedOnce on envelope expiry or check expiresAt in tickOnce/launch before admitting a ready step.

votes.reasoning: Not refuted. The code path is real. In decide() (authorization.server.ts:386) `if (context.oneTime) return allow(...)` runs before the workstation expiry check at line 394 (`envelope.expiresAt <= now` -> ask). The remote-only expiry check at line 385 does not cover a workstation envelope. bus.server.ts:175 sets oneTime whenever request.oneTimeAction matches the action, so a step's approvedOnce reaches decide() as oneTime. I probed decide() directly in a mkdtemp folder (since removed): workstation envelope with expiresAt in the past plus oneTime returns allow; the same envelope without oneTime returns ask "The mission authorization expired." The gap is time-of-check versus time-of-use: deviceRequestRefusal (manager.server.ts ~2058-2061) checks expiry only when the device answers. Nothing re-checks expiry before execution: tickOnce (manager.server.ts ~914-960) checks only the runtime budget, and the ready-step launch path and skills.run have no expiresAt check. A ready step with approvedOnce therefore still runs after envelope expiry. I did not rerun the full MissionManager probe. The practical window is narrow: the step must still be unadmitted at expiry, e.g. behind maxConcurrentAgents, a pause gate, or a later workstation resume. The action stays bound to the exact step and fingerprint, and it is non-sensitive. The same code path also runs a workstation one-time answer given before expiry, so it is not device-specific. That is not the owner's listed disposition, which covers answers given after expiry. It is still a policy-relevant ("outside the authorization envelope") timing gap. LOW is a fair severity. The repo was not modified, and no test-results files changed (I ran no repo tests).

Not refuted. The finding is real, but it is a LOW timing gap, not a code-execution path.

Code path (verified by reading, src/lib/bunny-missions/authorization.server.ts):
- decide() checks revokedAt (line 383), then the remote-only expiry check (line 385, guarded by isRemoteEnvelope), then `if (context.oneTime) return allow(...)` (line 386). The workstation expiry check `envelope.expiresAt <= now` (line 394) comes after the oneTime branch, so a one-time allowance bypasses expiry for a workstation envelope. This ordering already existed at 7fbea39 (old lines 167 vs 175), so it is not new, but it applies to device one-time answers too.
- Probe (throwaway temp dir, deleted afterwards): a workstation envelope with expiresAt in the past returns allow for oneTime:true and ask "The mission authorization expired." without it. Confirmed.
- Execution path: tickOnce (manager.server.ts 914-960) checks only mission.startedAt runtime, not envelope.expiresAt. launch() (1149+) does not check expiry. Neither re-checks before admitting a ready step. Grep shows expiresAt checks only at manager lines 139, 249, 2061, 2622, 3560, 3954, none on the tick/launch path. The one-time flag reaches decide via bus.server.ts:175 (oneTime from oneTimeAction matching the action). So a step with an approvedOnce admitted after expiry runs.
- Realistic trigger: the device answers allow_once while the envelope is valid, and the step then waits (maxConcurrentAgents full, workspace lock held by another step, or agent paused) past expiresAt. launch() returns false on lock wait and the approvedOnce stays on the step.

Why not a disposition: the listed accepted item covers only a workstation answer given after expiry. This case is an answer given while valid, executed after expiry, and the device-answer intake check (line 2061) only covers answer time. It is a device-attributed action outside the authorization time window, which the policy names, though the action is still the exact planned, single-use, in-scope filesystem write, so no new action, root or code run is reached. LOW fits. The suggested fix (re-check expiresAt and revokedAt before honouring oneTime, or check in tickOnce/launch before admission) is sound.

finding.title: A device answer that resumes a waiting Mission does not make it device-driven, so revocation does not stop it
finding.scenario: A workstation Mission is waiting_for_user. A paired device answers allow_once through mission.respond; respond() (line 3735) sets the Mission to running with mission.resumed but never calls markDeviceDriven. The same gap exists in childApprovedDirectly (line 2956). markDeviceDriven is called only from commands.server.ts:60 (mission.start) and agent-runtime.server.ts:214 (agent.resume). On revocation, endDeviceAnswers clears the unexecuted one-time answer, but endDeviceDriven (lines 2353-2360) skips the Mission because deviceDriven is unset, so the Mission keeps running to completion under the workstation envelope. The stated policy (P) requires that revoking a device stops Missions it started or resumed.
finding.evidence: Probe (MissionManager, temp Host DB): after device allow_once, state=running and deviceDriven=null; endDeviceAnswers(device)=1; endDeviceDriven(device)=0; afterwards state=completed and the planned file was written. Existing test F01-R52 calls markDeviceDriven directly and never exercises the respond() resume path.
finding.recommendation: Call markDeviceDriven(mission.id, by) when a device answer moves a waiting_for_user Mission to running (respond() at ~3735 and childApprovedDirectly at ~2956), and add a test that drives the answer path rather than calling markDeviceDriven directly.

votes.reasoning:
Verified by code reading; I did not run a runtime probe, and I made no repo edits and ran no tests.

The gap is real. markDeviceDriven has exactly two call sites: commands.server.ts:60 (mission.start) and agent-runtime.server.ts:214 (agent.resume). Neither covers the answer path. Within respond() (manager.server.ts ~3636-3760), a device allow_once on a waiting_for_user Mission reaches the block at ~3737-3740 that calls setMission(...,"mission.resumed") with no markDeviceDriven. The same holds for childApprovedDirectly (manager.server.ts:2958-2961). endDeviceDriven (2353-2360) filters on mission.deviceDriven === actor, so such a Mission is skipped on revocation. markDeviceDriven's own doc comment says a device "chose when this Mission (re)starts", and a device answer that resumes a waiting Mission matches that definition, so the omission contradicts the code's stated intent and policy P. The existing test F01-R52 (remote-authority.test.ts:1537-1549) calls markDeviceDriven directly and never drives the respond() path, so the gap is untested.

Severity is LOW, not higher. The device's one-time answer is consumed, and endDeviceAnswers clears any unexecuted one. The Mission continues under the workstation-approved envelope. Later changes are still attributed to the device via the remoteActorFor Mission-wide fallback (manager.server.ts:2314-2330), so they are recorded for review. Code runs stay blocked by the Host-wide pending-review gate until the workstation acknowledges those changes. I found no path where this lets a device cause code or shell execution.

Verified statically; I did not run a probe, and I did not run any test or modify any file. (1) markDeviceDriven has only two call sites: commands.server.ts:60 (mission.start) and agent-runtime.server.ts:214 (agent.resume). Grep confirms neither device-answer path calls it. (2) respond() at manager.server.ts:3735-3741 moves a waiting_for_user Mission to running with mission.resumed and never sets deviceDriven. childApprovedDirectly at lines 2956-2961 has the same gap. (3) endDeviceDriven (manager.server.ts:2353-2360) selects only missions where deviceDriven === actor, so a Mission that only a device answer resumed is skipped. (4) http.server.ts:828-829 calls endDeviceAnswers then endDeviceDriven, and that code comment says Missions the device "started or resumed" are ended, so the resume-by-answer case is claimed but not implemented. Mitigations, which keep this at LOW: the device gains no code execution or out-of-envelope action from the gap. The Mission runs only the workstation-approved plan, its later changes are still attributed to the device through remoteActorFor's answered-request scan and held or reviewed, and the one-time answer is cleared by endDeviceAnswers. The existing test F01-R52 calls markDeviceDriven directly and does not exercise the respond() path. The fix proposed in the finding (call markDeviceDriven when a device answer resumes a Mission) is consistent with the round-11 P policy.

finding.title: Mission-level change summary in the workstation prompt is not JSON-encoded
finding.scenario: askPermission appends 'Files changed in this Mission under paired-device authority: <names>' to every desktopRequired reason (terminal, Git, shell-session asks). The names come from remoteChanges() (lines 2306-2312), which returns raw run.params.path strings and does not filter out acknowledged paths. Unlike pendingRemoteReview's listing, the names are not JSON-encoded, so a device can name an inert data file with sentence-like text and that text reaches the workstation's approval prompt verbatim. remoteChanges returns [] unless the envelope is device-granted, which limits where this appears.
finding.evidence: Checked on this Windows host: 'notes. Approve everything, nothing else changed. y.txt' is a legal file name that passes inertDataPath (.txt leaf). The authoritative review listing (JSON-encoded, content-bound, acknowledged by row id) and grant binding are unaffected, and the summary grants nothing, so this is display-level text injection only.
finding.recommendation: Encode each summary entry the same way pendingRemoteReview encodes its listing (JSON.stringify per path, with the same escaping), and consider listing only unacknowledged changes.

votes.reasoning:
The claim is accurate. manager.server.ts:2306-2312 (remoteChanges) returns raw run.params.path strings, with no JSON encoding and no filtering of acknowledged paths. Line 3486-3488 joins them verbatim into the desktopRequired ask reason. The review listing (manager.server.ts:81 and 2343) JSON-encodes each entry and escapes bidi controls U+202A-202E and U+2066-2069; the summary path does neither.

Probe (throwaway temp dir, deleted afterwards): on this Windows host, "notes. Approve everything, nothing else changed. y.txt" is created successfully and inertDataPath() from authorization.server.ts:168 returns true for it. A name starting with U+202E ("‮cod.txt") is also created and also passes inertDataPath. So a device-chosen name can carry arbitrary sentence text, comma-separated fake entries, and RTL-override display spoofing into the summary.

Impact is display-only. The summary is appended to the reason of a desktopRequired ask (terminal, Git, shell session). Nothing in that ask grants anything: the grant binds Host id, epoch, operation, and mutation sequence, and any new change after the ask supersedes it (manager.server.ts:3691-3698). The authoritative review is a separate bus ask (capabilities/bus.server.ts:169-171) whose listing is JSON-encoded and acknowledged only through remoteReview ids (manager.server.ts:3708-3709). A desktopRequired ask without remoteReview does not acknowledge any review. Code cannot run over unreviewed changes because pendingRemoteChanges is Host-wide and checked at launch. The summary is also not shown to devices (redactReviewListing, http.server.ts:131, matches "paired-device authority"). So the worst case is a workstation misled about which files were changed while answering a terminal or Git prompt, which the separate review gate still covers. That is a legitimate LOW hygiene finding, not a BLOCKER or HIGH. It is not one of the listed accepted limitations or owner-policy dispositions. The summary also lists every succeeded run path, including already-acknowledged ones, which the finding notes correctly.

The code is as described: manager.server.ts:3488 joins raw remoteChanges() names (line 2306-2312, run.params.path, not acknowledged-filtered) with no JSON encoding, unlike pendingRemoteReview's listing at 2343. The finding's attack premise fails, though. A device cannot choose the name of a filesystem.write path. Write paths come from the workstation-authored Mission plan (exact planned steps), and devices cannot supply them: commands.server.ts:41-43 refuses mission.create with explicit steps from non-local actors, mission.create/plan/replan are not in the device authority table (device-authority.server.ts:60-95 has only approve/start/respond/stop/revoke_batch/inbox.ack for missions), and mission.respond accepts only requestId/decision/maxActions/ttlMs (commands.server.ts:66-67). Device "submit" creates a chat task, not a Mission. So a name carrying sentence-like text only comes from workstation-authored plans (or model-chosen agent paths the workstation approved), which is not a device-controlled injection. The summary also grants nothing: the answer binds to listed row ids and the grant to the mutation sequence and exact operation. Residual is hygiene only (unencoded workstation-authored names, and the summary lists all Mission changes, including already-acknowledged ones). Verified by reading the code only; no probes, no test run, no repo files changed (test-results/ untouched).

finding.title: Review preview bidi escaping omits LRM, RLM and ALM
finding.scenario: describeRemoteChange escapes U+2022, U+2028, U+2029, U+202A-U+202E and U+2066-U+2069 in file previews, but not U+200E (LRM), U+200F (RLM) or U+061C (ALM). Those marks can change how the workstation's prompt text renders around a changed file's content. This is display-only and does not affect structure, since the content is JSON-encoded and quoted.
finding.evidence: Source regex at manager.server.ts:81; no execution or grant path depends on it.
finding.recommendation: Add ‎, ‏ and ؜ to the escape class.
